title: 8  Recovering deleted commits
text:
8.1 When does Git actually delete an object?
When using Git, you will inevitable end up in a situation where you accidentally “delete” one or more commits, for example by deleting a branch before integrating the changes into the main code. The good news is, that the “deleted” commits are almost never truly gone, and they can be recovered. In this chapter we will introduce the reference log, also called reflog, which we can use to recover lost commits.

title: 8  Recovering deleted commits
text:
If you delete a branch with commits that have not been integrated into the main code, the only thing you have done is deleting the reference to a specific commit, i.e. the pointer to the tip of a series of commits. The commit objects are still in the Git database, but they are now unreachable: they are not ancestors of any commits that are on a branch. From time to time Git will delete unnecessary (unreachable) commits and optimize the repository when it deems it necessary, but this only happens when you do specific operations or after a long period of time in very large repositories. If you want to recover a lost commit, you can always do this as long as you do so right after accidentally “deleting them”.





Unreachable commits on a deleted branch

title: 8  Recovering deleted commits
section: 8.2 Identifying and recovering unreachable commits using the reference log
text:
8.2 Identifying and recovering unreachable commits using the reference log
To recover a lost commit, the first step is to recover the SHA-1 checksum of that commit. Since this commit is now unreachable, we can not use git log <branch> to find the SHA-1 checksum, since git log <branch> only includes reachable commits from the tip of a branch. But Git has another tool that can help us: the reference log, or just reflog, which has its own command, git reflog. The reflog logs all changes to a reference that has happened over time, meaning that every time a reference is changed to point to something else, this is logged. Let’s see how this looks like in practice by creating a repository with the same history as illustrated above: a main branch with two commits, and a feature branch with a single commit off of main, where we delete the feature branch before integrating the changes into main:
$ mkdir ~/reflog-example
$ cd ~/reflog-example
$ git init
$ echo "Content of C1" > file.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"C1"
$ echo "Content of C2" >> file.txt
$ git commit -am"C2"
$ git switch -c feature
$ echo "Content of C3" >> file.txt
$ git commit -am"C3"
$ git switch main
$ git branch -D feature
$ git log --oneline --all --graph
* 6891983 (HEAD -> main) C2
* a961cba C1

After deleting feature, we can no longer see the commits on that branch. If we run git reflog however, we can recover the branch:
$ git reflog
6891983 (HEAD -> main) HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from feature to main
b2d535d HEAD@{1}: commit: C3
6891983 (HEAD -> main) HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from main to feature
6891983 (HEAD -> main) HEAD@{3}: commit: C2
a961cba HEAD@{4}: commit (initial): C1

By default, git reflog shows the reference log of HEAD. The format HEAD @{x}, means where was HEAD x moves ago. So HEAD@{0} means where is HEAD right now, HEAD@{1} means where was HEAD one move ago, and so one. From the reflog we can se that one move ago, HEAD was pointing to the C3 commit, the tip of the former feature branch, and we can see the SHA1 checksum of that commit is b2d535d. Now we can recover the feature branch simply by making a new branch pointing to that commit:
$ git branch feature b2d535d
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
* b2d535d (feature) C3
* 6891983 (HEAD -> main) C2
* a961cba C1

title: 10  Using git diff to show code changes
text:
10.1 Show changes in the working tree - Understanding the git diff output
A diff is a program that compares the content of files or directories, line by line, and shows the differences between them. Git comes with its own diff command, git diff, which can be used to compare different states of a repository. Using diffs allows developers to inspect changes before adding them to the index or making a commit, compare changes made in a feature branch with your main branch before merging and so on, which is an essential skill to learn when using Git.
This chapter will focus under understanding the output that git diff produces and introducing some of the most common ways diffs are used in Git. As always, we will only scratch the surface of what is possible to do.
Using git diff with no arguments will show changes made in the working tree that has not yet been staged for the next commit. More precisely, Git compares the working tree and the index. This invocation of git diff can be used to see exactly what changes would be added to the index if git add was used.
Let’s explore this with an example where we also go through how to interpret the output that git diff provides. First, let’s initiate a Git repository where we create a file, add it to the index, and use git diff:
Since we have not added any changes to the working tree after adding file1.txt to the index, the state of file1.txt is the same in the working tree and the index, so git diff produces no output. Now, let’s add some changes to file1.txt and run git diff again:
The output that git diff produces is quite technical, so lets go through it line by line.
crumbs: 10  Using `git diff` to show code changes

title: 10  Using git diff to show code changes
text:
$ mkdir ~/example-git-diff
$ cd ~/example-git-diff
$ git init
$ echo "Content in index" > file1.txt
$ git add .
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached ..." to unstage)
        new file:   file1.txt

$ git diff



$ echo "New content in working tree" >> file1.txt
$ git diff
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index fc997de..ed98e30 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 Content in index
+New content in working tree



Structure of git diff output
For each file being compared, Git groups changes into “hunks”, sections of the file that contains changes, which are presented separately. In this simple example we only have one file with a few lines, so there is only one hunk in the output.


The header
The first line
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt

in each hunk is called the header. It is informing us what inputs has been given to the diff. We can see that two versions of file1.txt has been passed to the diff, a/file1.txt and b/file1.txt. It looks like Git is comparing two files with the file paths a/file1.txt and b/file1.txt, which is not the case. Git is just informing us, in a somewhat confusing way, that the first input has been assigned the symbol “a” and the second input has been assigned the symbol “b”. In this example where we have called git diff with no arguments, the first input “a” is the version of file1.txt in the index, and “b” is the version of file1.txt in the working tree. You can think of version “a” as the “old” or “original” version of the file, and “b” as the “new” or “modified” version of the file. Again, this makes sense in our current example where we want to see the changes in the working tree not yet added to the index: the old version is the version in the index, and the new version is the version in the working tree.
The start of the line diff --git might look like that Git has run the BASH command diff with a --git flag, but this is not actually the case. This is just Git’s way of telling us that the diff has been produced by Git’s own internal diff function.


Git meta data
The second line
index fc997de..ed98e30 100644

displays some Git metadata. The first word “index” in this context does not refer to the index/staging area in Git, but is instead indicating that what follows is an indexed identifier of the data being compared. The next two words are (abbreviated) SHA-1 hash identifiers that Git uses to refer to the specific versions of the content being compared. So “fc997de” is the SHA-1 hash of file1.txt version in the index, and “ed98e30” is the SHA-1 hash of version of file1.txt in the working tree. We can check this by manually computing the checksum of the two different versions of the file:
# SHA-1 hash of file1.txt in index
$ git ls-files -s file1.txt
100644 fc997ded06b626fcc07db7da1e3a7bbf4e7349d4 0       file1.txt
# SHA-1 hash of file1.txt in working tree
$ git hash-object file1.txt
ed98e302716a8f7df192d2e7474f8ee96b13c35b

The two dots “..” between the given SHA-1 identifiers represents a range from one state to another. You can think of “fc997de..ed98e30” as “the difference between fc997de and ed98e30”. Finally, the last word “100644” is some technical jargon that means that the file is a normal, non-executable file.


Markers for changes
The next lines
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt

are a legend that assigns symbols to diff input sources. In this case, changes from version “a” of the file is marked with a “—”, and changes from version “b” is marked with a “+++” symbol.


The hunk header
The next line
@@ -1 +1,2 @@

is the “hunk header”. It is a summary of shown lines from the files being compared. The “@” symbols marks the beginning and end of the hunk header. It serves as a delimiter that Git uses to identify the hunk header.

-1 - This indicates the lines shown from the original file (the version in the index), denoted by the -. The 1 signifies that the shown lines are from line 1 to the end of the file.
+1,2 - This part indicates lines shown from the updated file (the version in the working tree), denoted by the “+” symbol. Here the 1 indicates that the lines shown begin from the first line in the file, and 2 means that from that starting point, there are two lines shown from the updated file, including the first line, that is, the lines 1 and 2 are the two lines.

This is arguably the most confusing part of the diff output, and takes some effort to understand correctly. We will talk more about the hunk header in later, more complicated examples, but it not essential to have a perfect understanding of the hunk header, and we will not delve too much on the precise interpretation of this information 1.


The diff content
The remaining output
 Content in index
+New content in working tree

is the diff content, and consists of three different types of diff lines.

Context lines: Lines that have not changed between the two versions. These lines help you understand where in the file changes are happening. By default, these lines are shown in grey. In our example, the “Content in index” line is a context line, since it is present in both versions of the file. These lines are not preceded by any symbol.
Deletion lines: Lines that were present in version “a”, the old version, but are not present in the new version, “b”. These lines are preceded by a “-”. By default, these lines are shown in red. Our current example does not contain any deletion lines.
Addition lines: Lines that are present in version “b”, the new version, but were not present in version “a”, the old version. These lines are preceded by a “+”. By default, these lines are shown in green. In our example, “New content in working tree” is an addition line.

The diff content essentially provides a before-and-after snapshot of your file. You can see the context (what part of the file remained unchanged), the deletions (what parts were removed from the old version), and the additions (what parts were added in the new version). As indicated by the colors and symbols, you can think of the diff content as a chunk of changes in the file, with some context lines around changes to provide context, red deletion lines indicating what lines have been removed from the original file, and green addition lines showing what has been added in the modified version.


Continuation of example
Let’s expand our example now that we understand the output from git diff. First, let’s add the “New content in working tree” line to the index, and commit file1.txt to the repository:
# Current state of file1.txt in the working directory
$ cat file1.txt
Content in index
New content in working tree
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Add file1.txt"

Yet again, let’s add some changes to file1.txt in the working tree and use git diff:
$ echo "Changes after commit" >> file1.txt
$ git diff
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index ed98e30..e283c5a 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
 Content in index
 New content in working tree
+Changes after commit

First of all, it might be surprising why this is showing any output at all. As stated before, git diff compares the working tree and the index, but we have not added anything to the index, so why is Git telling us that the line “Changes after commit” is in the file1.txt version in the working space, but not in the version of the file in the index? Why is it not producing no output as when we initially made changes in the working tree and used git diff before adding anything to the index? This is because we have made a commit in the meantime. The index keeps track of all files it knows about, and since we have made a commit where we added file1.txt to the repository, the index is currently containing information on the version of file1.txt that was last commited. So, if we have not staged anything since our last commit, we can actually use git diff to compare the state of the working tree with the latest commit on the active branch, if the files are already tracked by Git! We can show this more clearly by adding a new file in the working tree and running git diff again:
$ echo "Content of file2.txt" > file2.txt
$ git diff
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index ed98e30..e283c5a 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
 Content in index
 New content in working tree
+Changes after commit

We can see that git diff still only show the changes in file1.txt in the working tree, since Git is not currently tracking file2.txt, so the index does not contain any information on that file.
Looking at the git diff output, we can see that the output is easier to understand now: The “-1,2” part of the hunk header is telling us that the diff lines are showing the two first lines of the version of file1.txt from the index, namely the lines “Content in index” and “New content in the working tree”, both of which are context lines since they are also present in the version in the working tree. The “+1,3” is additionally telling us that the 3 first lines are shown from the version of file1.txt in the working tree with the two same context lines and the addition line “Changes after commit”.
Let’s wrap up this example by deleting the repository:
$ cd
$ rm -rf ~/example-git-diff

title: 10  Using git diff to show code changes
text:
10.2 Compare index with latest commit
Another common way to use git diff is to compare the index to the latest commit on the active branch, by using the --staged flag. This invocation of git diff can be used to see exactly what changes are committed before using git commit.
Let’s illustrate this with a new example. First we initialize a repository with a single commit of two files:
$ mkdir ~/example-git-diff2
$ cd ~/example-git-diff2
$ git init
$ echo "Content in file1.txt" > file1.txt
$ echo "Content in file2.txt" > file2.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Add file1.txt and file2.txt"

Now, we make changes to both files, but we only add the changes to file1.txt to the index, and then we use git diff --staged:
$ echo "More content in file1.txt" >> file1.txt
$ echo "More content in file2.txt" >> file2.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged ..." to unstage)
        modified:   file1.txt

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add ..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore ..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   file2.txt

$ git diff --staged
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index a1b2117..b00037e 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 Content in file1.txt
+More content in file1.txt

We can see that we are indeed only shown the changes to file1.txt that would be added to the repository if we were to use git commit at this point, and that we are not shown the changes to file1.txt in the working tree which has not been added to the index.
Let’s wrap up by deleting the example folder:
$ cd
$ rm -rf ~/example-git-diff2

title: 10  Using git diff to show code changes
text:
10.3 Compare two commits
It is also possible to diff two commits, to see the differences between them using git diff <commit> <commit>, where <commit> is the (abbreviated) SHA-1 checksum of a commit object. One of the most common uses of this form of git diff is git diff HEAD^ HEAD which shows changes introduced in the most recent commit on the active branch. As you might recall, HEAD, is just a pointer to the most recent commit on the active branch, and HEAD^ is the parent commit of HEAD. This is a neat way to make the comparison of interest without having to type out tedious and hard to remember checksums in the terminal. This also illustrates that we can use refs to refer to commits, instead of actual commit checksums in the call to git diff. This means that we compare branches with the same type of call eg git diff main feature_a to see what changes has been introduced in a feature branch before we merge it to our main branch.
Again, let’s illustrate this with an example. First we create a repository with a series of commits, making changes to a single file:
$ mkdir ~/example-git-diff3
$ cd ~/example-git-diff3
$ git init
$ echo "Content added in commit A" > file1.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Commit A"
$ echo "Content added in commit B" >> file1.txt
$ git commit -am"Commit B"
$ echo "Content added in commit C" >> file1.txt
$ git commit -am"Commit C"
$ git log --oneline
d32fc58 (HEAD -> main) Commit C
9b4a089 Commit B
cd80503 Commit A

As previously explained, if we want to see the changes introduced in the newest commit, Commit C, we can do it in two ways. We can either specify the commit checksums directly, or we can use the git diff HEAD^ HEAD form:
$ git diff HEAD^ HEAD
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index e8e75be..419b45c 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
 Content added in commit A
 Content added in commit B
+Content added in commit C

$diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index e8e75be..419b45c 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
 Content added in commit A
 Content added in commit B
+Content added in commit C git diff 9b4a098 d32fc58 

We can see that we get the exact same results, but that the git diff HEAD^ HEAD form of using git diff is much easier to use.
Let’s continue the example by making a branch, and making a commit on that branch:
$ git switch -c feature_a
$ echo "Content added on feature_a branch" >> file1.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Update file1.txt"
$ git log --oneline
8b8e809 (HEAD -> feature_a) Update file1.txt
d32fc58 (main) Commit C
9b4a089 Commit B
cd80503 Commit A

Let’s say we want to merge the feature branch into the main branch, but that we want to see exactly what changes we would be adding before we do so. Again we could explictly compare commit ID’s, or we could simply specify the branch names in the git diff command:
$ git diff d32fc58 8b8e809
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index 419b45c..89b6cb2 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@
 Content added in commit A
 Content added in commit B
 Content added in commit C
+Content added on feature_a branch

$ git diff main feature_a
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index 419b45c..89b6cb2 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@
 Content added in commit A
 Content added in commit B
 Content added in commit C
+Content added on feature_a branch

Again we see that we get identical results, but it is much easier to refer to the commits with branch references.
To wrap up the example we delete the repository:

text:
10.4 Exercises
TODO: The main purpose of the exercises should be to expand on the introduced types of diffs with more complicated example with multiple files, chunks of changes etc.

Exercise 1 - Compare files outside a Git repository
In this chapter we have focused on comparing differences in objects in a Git repository. But you can actually also diff two random files on your computer outside of a Git repository using git diff <path> <path>, where <path> is a path to a file on your filesystem.
Imagine you are part of a research group that is writing an article. The previous version of the article draft, article_draft_v2.txt is updated by the first author, and you want to get an overview of the exact changes that have been introduced in the new version, article_draft_v3.txt2.
Use the following commands to generate the files for the exercise (Consider copy+pasting the echo commands into the terminal to avoid spelling errors):
$ mkdir ~/git-diff-ex1
$ echo -e "Introduction\nMethods\nResults\nDiscussion\nConclusion" > ~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v2.txt
$ echo -e "Abstract\nIntroduction\nMethods\nResults\nDiscussion\nConclusion\nSupplementary analyses" > ~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v3.txt
$ cat ~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v2.txt
Introduction
Methods
Results
Discussion
Conclusion
$ cat ~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v3.txt
Abstract
Introduction
Methods
Results
Discussion
Conclusion
Supplementary analyses

1. Make a diff of the two files
Use git diff <path> <path> to make a diff of article_draft_v2.txt and article_draft_v3.txt. Remember to use the full paths to each files, and use article_draft_v2.txt as the first input.






NoteSolution





$ git diff ~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v2.txt ~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v3.txt
diff --git a/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v2.txt b/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v3.txt
index b266301..e554467 100644
--- a/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v2.txt
+++ b/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v3.txt
@@ -1,5 +1,7 @@
+Abstract
 Introduction
 Methods
 Results
 Discussion
 Conclusion
+Supplementary analyses




2. Understanding the output
Go through the git diff output and consider what each part of the output means.






NoteSolution





The header
The first line of the output
diff --git a/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v2.txt b/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v3.txt

is the header.

“diff --git”: Git is telling us that the diff is made with Git
“a/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v2.txt”: First input which is assigned the symbol “a” and treated as the “old” version.
“a/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v3.txt”: Second input which is assigned the symbol “b” and treated as the “new” version.

Git meta data
The second line of the output
index b266301..e554467 100644

is the Git meta data.

“index”: This does not refer to the staging area in this context, but instead is used to to tell us that what follows is indexed identifiers of the data being compared.
“b266301”: (abbreviated) SHA-1 checksum of the first input. We can check this by hashing the file ourselves:

$ git hash-object ~/git-diff-ex1/folder1/file1.txt
b2663016d267a1ab40f4555dd731715c1fe5bba6


“e554467”: (abbreviated) SHA-1 checksum of the second input. We can check this by hashing the file ourselves:

$ git hash-object ~/git-diff-ex1/folder2/file2.txt
e554467d786e0a61ce9943be4e666d3618c6dd42


“..”: The two dots between the SHA-1 checksums represents a range from one state to another. We can think of this as Git telling us that it is finding the differences between objects b266301 and e554467.
“100644”: Just some technical jargon telling us that the files being compared are normal non-executable files.

Markers for changes
The third and fourth line of the output
--- a/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v2.txt
+++ b/~/git-diff-ex1/article_draft_v3.txt

is a legend that assigns symbols to the different input sources. Here, changes from article_draft_v2.txt is given the symbol "---", and changes from article_draft_v3.txt is given the symbol “+++”.
Hunk header
The sixth line of the output
@@ -1,5 +1,7 @@

is the hunk header. The hunk header is a summary of lines shown from the two inputs being compared.

“@” symbols: marks the beginning and end of the hunk header.
“-1,5”: Indicates what lines are shown from the first input / “old” version in the diff content. Here, we are informed that starting from the first line of the file, 5 lines are shown, including the first line.
“+1.7”: Indicates what lines are shown from the second input / “new” version in the diff content. Here, we are informed that that starting from the first line of the file, 7 lines are shown, including the first line.

Diff lines
The remaining lines of of the output
+Abstract
 Introduction
 Methods
 Results
 Discussion
 Conclusion
+Supplementary analyses

is the diff content. There are no red deletion lines, meaning that nothing has from article_draft_v2.txt has been removed in article_draft_v3.txt. There are two green addition lines, meaning that two lines have been added in article_draft_v3.txt that were not present in article_draft_v2.txt. Finally, several grey context lines are included in the output, giving context to where in article_draft_v3.txt lines have been added.



Wrap up by deleting the files created for the exercise:
$ cd
$ rm -rf ~/git-diff-ex1



Exercise 2 - Multiple diff hunks
So far we have only looked at examples where there is a single diff hunk in the output from git diff, showing all lines from the diffed file. If the file being diffed is very long and has changes that are very far apart, Git is not going to show the entire file but will instead separate the changes into multiple diff hunks, showing only a few context lines around changes in each hunk. If multiple files are being diffed, there would also be at least one diff hunk for each file.
Run the following commands to set-up a Git repository with a commit of two files, with additional changes in the worktree to the files after the commit:
$ mkdir ~/git-diff-ex2
$ cd ~/git-diff-ex2
$ git init
$ echo "Content of file1" > file1.txt
$ echo "Content of file2" > file2.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Initial commit of file1.txt and file2.txt"
$ echo "Additional content" >> file1.txt
$ echo "Additional content" >> file2.txt

1. Make a diff of worktree and index
Make a diff of the worktree and the index.






NoteSolution





To make a diff of the worktree and the index, we can simply use git diff with no arguments:
$ git diff
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index 65e756a..e24b6bc 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 Content of file1
+Additional content
diff --git a/file2.txt b/file2.txt
index aad9de2..6541eda 100644
--- a/file2.txt
+++ b/file2.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 Content of file2
+Additional content




2. Identify each diff hunk
Go through the output of the diff and identify each diff hunk.






NoteSolution





Each hunk starts with a header starting with “diff --git”.



Wrap up by deleting the files created for the exercise:
$ cd
$ rm -rf ~/git-diff-ex2

title: 11  Introduction to GitHub
text:
11.1 Create a GitHub account and install the GitHub CLI
GitHub is a web-based service that hosts Git repositories. Simply put, you can host a remote of your Git repository on GitHub instead of having a remote locally on your network. This makes it possible for you to access your Git repository from any computer with an internet connection, which is obviously beneficial. But GitHub is also much more than that. GitHub offers many features that facilitate collaboration, and can be used for much more than simply storing your repository on the internet. It is outside the scope of this tutorial to go into much detail about what GitHub can be used for and how, since it would quickly become an entire tutorial in itself, but we will introduce and illustrate some basic features that should make it clear how valuable a tool GitHub can be.
GitHub has a web user-interface that is easy to navigate and use, and is most likely the easiest way to to interact with your GitHub account and your repositories for most people, especially if you are not comfortable using a CLI. But illustrating how to use the web user-interface in a tutorial with an enormous amount of screenshots, is most certainly not the best way to learn how to use GitHub. Because of this, and in line with the philosophy of this tutorial, we will instead opt to use the GitHub CLI to interact with GitHub from the command line. This will work just as well for the simple features we will introduce in this tutorial, but there might be some advanced features that are not possible to use through the GitHub CLI, or it simply easier to do through the web user-interface. Keep this in mind if you want to use GitHub in the future. There is plenty of documentation on the GitHub website on how to use the web-interface.
To do basically anything other than browsing and cloning repositories on GitHub, you need to create an account. You can create a free GitHub account by going to https://github.com and sign up.
As stated, we will interact with GitHub from the command line using the GitHub CLI. You can install it from Git BASH by running the following command:
This should work from git BASH. If not, try running the command in PowerShell. Alternatively, download and install it from https://cli.github.com/.
You need to restart your terminal before you can use the GitHub CLI gh commands.

title: 11  Introduction to GitHub
text:
11.2 Authenticate with your GitHub account
The most technical aspect of using GitHub is to authenticate with your GitHub account. You need to do this to verify to GitHub that you are who you claim to be, so that you are allowed to access your GitHub account and push changes to your repositories etc. You can authenticate with your GitHub account from the command line using either HTTPS or SSH. It is outside the scope of this tutorial to go into any details about what this means, and to explain the pros and cons of each protocol. Here we will simply show how you can authenticate using HTTPS using the GitHub CLI. To authenticate with your GitHub account, run the following command:
$ gh auth login -p"https" -cw

Follow the link given in the terminal. If you are not logged into your GitHub account already, you will be prompted to do so first. Then you will be asked to enter the one-time code that was provided in the terminal output (which should already be copied to the clipboard). You should only need to do this once for each machine you work on.1
The rest of this chapter assumes that you have created a GitHub account, and have authenticated with it to allow you to access and modify your repositories.

title: 11  Introduction to GitHub
text:
11.3 Licenses
Before talking about how to host repositories on GitHub, we need to talk briefly about licences. If you put a repository on GitHub to share it with others, you should include a license that specifies what other people can do with your code. You are not obligated to include a license, but if you don’t, default copyright laws apply, meaning that you retain all rights to your source code and no one may reproduce, distribute, or create derivative works from your work. This might not be what you want. GitHub strongly encourages you to include an open source licence, the MIT licence being a common choice. The MIT licence is a short permissive software license, that basically allows people to do whatever they want with your code, as long as they include the original copyright and licence in any copy of the code. Also, the licence states that you hold zero liability for use of the code. In many cases, this is a very reasonable license, and a good default choice. If you want to to learn more about licences, here are few resources that might be of interest:
https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/licensing-a-repository
https://opensource.guide/legal/#which-open-source-license-is-appropriate-for-my-project
https://choosealicense.com
https://www.tldrlegal.com

title: 11  Introduction to GitHub
text:
11.4 Creating a repository on GitHub
There are two ways to get a repository on GitHub. You can either initialize a new project directly on GitHub, or you can upload a repository to GitHub from an existing local repository. If you are starting a new Git repository and you want to have a remote on GitHub, you have two choices: Initialize the repository on GitHub and clone it, or initialize the repository locally, and then upload it to GitHub. There is no right or wrong way to do this, it comes down to personal preferences.
You can initialize or upload a Git repository on GitHub using the gh repo create [<name>] [flags] command. You can find documentation on this command at https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create, or you can use gh repo create --help in the terminal. It is possible to create a repository interactively in the terminal by running gh repo create with no arguments, but that is not something we will explore here. Instead we will create repositories non-interactively, and in this case we need, as a minimum, to specify a name for the repository and use flags to specify if the repository is to be (--public) or private (--private). Public repositories can be seen by everyone, whereas private repositories can only been seen by yourself.

Initialize a new Git repository on GitHub
Let’s illustrate how to initialize a new Git repository directly on GitHub. As mentioned before, besides giving the repository a name, we also need to to use a flag to specify whether the repository should be public or private. Furthermore, it is common practice to initialize a repository with an initial commit adding a README to the repository:
$ gh repo create init-on-github --public --add-readme

This creates a new public repository called init-on-github in your GitHub account with an empty README file.
You can now clone the repository, automatically setting up the repository on GitHub as a remote, and start working on the project:
$ cd ~
$ git clone "https://github.com/your-user-name/init-on-github"
$ cd init-on-github
$ git log --oneline
9caef1d (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) Initial commit
$ ls
README.md
$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/your-user-name/init-on-github (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/your-user-name/init-on-github (push)



Upload repository from existing local repository
Imagine you have the following Git repository set up locally:
$ mkdir ~/init-local-repo
$ cd ~/init-local-repo
$ git init
$ touch README.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Initial commit"

To upload the repository to GitHub, we can use gh repo create with the --source flag to specify a local repository to use as a source for the repository. Furthermore, we can use the --push flag to push the local commits to the GitHub repository, and use the --remote flag to specify the name for the remote:
$ gh repo create init-local-repo --public --source=. --remote=origin --push
$ git log --oneline
f662630 (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Initial commit
$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/your-user-name/init-local-repo (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/your-user-name/init-local-repo (push)

title: 11  Introduction to GitHub
text:
11.5 Tools to facilitate collaboration
GitHub has a ton of features that are useful when collaborating on a project. Here we will briefly touch on some basic uses of some of these features.

Issues
GitHub has a built-in tracking tool called “issues” that can be used to manage tasks, make bug report, request features to be implemented etc. You can think of GitHub issues as a collaborative to-do list or a message board directly attached to a repository, allowing developers and users to discuss and organize work.
The GitHub CLI has a bunch of commands related to issues. Here, we will illustrate how to do basic tasks like create, list, view, and close issues using the following commands:





Description
Command




Create an issue
gh issue create <issue-name>


List issues
gh issue list


View issue
gh issue view <issue-number>


Add comment to issue
gh issue comment <issue-number>


Close issue
gh issue close <issue-number>





A full list of GitHub CLI commands related to issues, optional flags, and how to use them can be found at https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue

Example
To illustrate how issues can be used, imagine a project with two collaborators that initiate and upload a repository they are going to work on to GitHub:
$ mkdir ~/issues-example
$ cd ~/issues-example
$ git init
$ echo "Project README" > README.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Initial commit"
$ gh repo create issues-example --public --source=. --remote=origin --push

Let’s say that collaborator A wants a feature implemented in the project. He communicate this to collaborator B by making an issue describing what he wants to implement:
$ gh issue create --title "Implement feature A" --body "Text describing what to add and how."

Collaborator B is notified (either directly by collaborator A or by a notification from GitHub) that collaborator A has created an issue in the repository, so he uses gh issue list to get an overview of the issues in the repository:
$ gh issue list

ID  TITLE                LABELS  UPDATED           
#1  Implement feature A          about 1 minute ago


He then uses gh issue view to get some more detailed information on the issue that collaborator A has made:
# Note that we are referring to the issue by its ID value
$ gh issue view 1
Implement feature A thomas-rasmussen/issues-example#1
Open • thomas-rasmussen opened about 1 hour ago • 0 comments


  Text describing what to add and how.


View this issue on GitHub: https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen/issues-example/issues/1


Collaborator B then adds a comment to the issue telling collaborator A to go ahead and implement the feature:
$ gh issue comment 1 --body "LGTM"

Collaborator A sees this, implements the feature in a feature branch, merge the changes into the main branch, and pushes the changes to the remote on GitHub:
$ git switch -c implement-feature-A
$ echo "Implementation of feature A" > feature_a.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit
$ git switch main
$ git merge implement-feature-A
$ git push
$ git branch -d implement-feature-A

Finally, collaborator A adds a comment to the issue saying that the feature has been added and pushed to the main branch, and then closes the issue:
$ gh issue comment 1 --body "Implemented and merged to main branch"
$ gh issue close 1

Let’s wrap up this example by deleting the GitHub repository:
$ gh repo delete issues-example --yes

You might not have permission to use this command. If this is the case run the following command and try again:
$ gh auth refresh -s delete_repo

We have only scraped the surface of what you can do with GitHub issues in this example, but it is hopefully clear how this tool can be valuable to organize work on a project.



Forks and pull requests
It is common to control which collaborators has write-access in a GitHub project. If everyone could push changes to the repository, the commit history could very quickly descend into chaos. Put if collaborators don’t have write-access, how are they supposed to contribute to the project? And in extension of that, how can you contribute to open-source projects on GitHub that you are not a part of? This is where forks and pull requests comes into play.
A fork is a copy of a repository that you own, connected to the original repository, called the upstream repository. A fork enables you to make changes in your own copy of the GitHub repository without affecting the upstream project, and when you are ready you can propose changes back to the upstream repository with a pull request. This is different than cloning a repository. If you clone a repository where you don’t have write-access, you won’t be able to push changes.
Pull requests are proposals to merge code changes into a project. The changes can be reviewed and commented upon in the pull request before they are merged into the repository by someone with write-access.

Example
Let’s imagine that we want to contribute to the GitHub repository github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example. First we make a fork of the repository and make a clone of the repository at the same time:
$ cd
$ gh repo fork thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example --clone

First of all, if we make a list of forked repositories on our account, we can see that a fork of git-tutorial-fork-example has been added:
gh repo list --fork

Showing 1 of 1 repositories in @user-name that match your search

NAME                                 DESCRIPTION                                            INFO          UPDATED         
user-name/git-tutorial-fork-example  Repository used to illustrate forking in Git tutorial  public, fork  about 3 days ago


Next we cd in to the local clone of the repository we also made, and inspect the remotes that have been automatically made:
$ cd git-tutorial-fork-example
$ git log --oneline
dd7b9d9 (HEAD -> main, upstream/main, upstream/HEAD, origin/main, origin/HEAD) Initial commit
$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (push)
upstream        https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (fetch)
upstream        https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen-alt/git-tutorial-fork-example.git (push)

We can see that two remote have been set up: one to the fork (origin) and one to the original/upstream (upstream) repository. Next, we make the changes we want to contribute to the original project in our local clone and push the changes to the fork:
$ git switch -c implement-feature
$ echo "Implementation of feature" > feature.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Implement feature"
$ git push
$ git log --oneline
d134f37 (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) Implement feature
dd7b9d9 (upstream/main, upstream/HEAD) Initial commit

Finally, we send a pull request to the original repository, asking them to merge our suggested changes:
$ gh pr create --title "Implement feature" --body "Implementation of important feature"

The proposed changes can then be reviewed/discussed in the pull request before the owner of the original repository can merge the changes when and if they want to. We will omit illustrating this final step in this tutorial.

title: 11  Introduction to GitHub
text:
11.6 GitHub pages
GitHub pages is a static site hosting service, that can take HTML, CSS, and Javascript files from a GitHub repository and turn them into a website. It is very simple to set up from a GitHub repository, and useful in a wide array of scenarios. Common use cases include:

Documentation
Personal websites
Blogs
Resumes

As an example, the tutorial you are currently reading is hosted as a static website on GitHub pages, based on the main branch of the repository that creates the tutorial. Every time the main branch is updated, the website is automatically updated!
It is outside the scope of this tutorial to go into details on how to use GitHub pages, but for more information see the official documentation at https://docs.github.com/en/pages

title: 11  Introduction to GitHub
text:
11.7 Exercises

Exercise 1 - Managing GitHub repositories using the GitHub CLI
In this exercise we will practice using some of the GitHub CLI commands that have been introduced in this chapter to illustrate how a simplified workflow using GitHub might look like.
Step 1 - Initialize a repository
Initialize a public repository directly on GitHub with an initial commit adding a README and a MIT license to the repository.






TipHint 1





You can find the gh repo create documentation at https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create









TipHint 2





Use the --license flag to add a license. You can find a list of available licences by running gh repo license list.









NoteSolution





$ gh repo create my-repo --public --add-readme --license=mit




Step 2 - Inspect repository
Before we clone the repository, we want to inspect how it looks like. Unfortunately, there is no easy way to list files, or contents of files, in a GitHub repository in the terminal. Instead, we want to open the repository in the browser, so we can take a closer look at it. Do this by navigation to the repository using the web UI, or use the gh repo view command.






TipHint





Use the --help flag to see the documentation for the gh repo view command.









NoteSolution





$ gh repo view my-repo --web




Step 3 - Clone the repository
Make a local clone and cd into the repository. Afterwards look at the commit history and list the files in it.






NoteSolution





$ cd
$ git clone https://github.com/user-name/my-repo.git
$ cd my-repo
$ git log --oneline
5f0b7da (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) Initial commit
$ ls
LICENSE  README.md




Step 4- Push change to repository
Commit a change in the main branch, and push it to the GitHub repository.






NoteSolution





$ echo "Add change" > file1.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Add change"
$ git push




Step 4 - Make an issue
Make an issue to implement a feature. Besides adding a title and description of the issue, assign the issue to yourself and add a label.






TipHint





Look at the gh issue create documentation at https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_create, or use the --help flag in the terminal.
You can find a list of valid label values at https://docs.github.com/en/issues/using-labels-and-milestones-to-track-work/managing-labels.









NoteSolution





$ gh issue create --title "Implement feature A" --body "Description of feature to be added" --assignee "@me" --label "enhancement"




Step 5 - Add comment in issue
Use gh issue comment to open the issue in the browser, and add a comment using the web UI. Start by using gh issue list to find the ID of the issue.






TipHint





Look at the documentation for the gh issue comment, using either the --help flag in the terminal, or by looking at the documentation at https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_comment









NoteSolution





$ gh issue list

Showing 1 of 1 open issue in user-name/my-repo

ID  TITLE                LABELS       UPDATED             
#1  Implement feature A  enhancement  about 51 minutes ago

$ gh issue comment --web"




Step 6 - Close issue
Close the issue with the gh issue close command using a flag to specify the issue was closed because it was completed.






TipHint





You can find the documentation for the gh issue close command at https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue_close, or you can use the --help flag to show the documentation in the terminal.









NoteSolution





$ gh issue close 1 --reason "completed"




Step 7 - Clean up
Delete the local clone and GitHub repository.






TipHint 1 - Deleting the repository





Look at the documentation for the gh issue commands at https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_issue or use gh issue --help to find a command that delete a GitHub repository.









TipHint 2 - Deleting the clone





To delete the local clone use the rm command. Make sure to use appropriate flags to recursively delete all folders and files in the repository folder.
If you are uneasy about using the rmcommand (which is not unreasonable), just delete the folder manually.









NoteSolution





$ gh repo delete my-repo --yes
$ cd
$ rm my-repo -rf






Exercise 2 - Contributing to an open-source project
In this exercise we will practice forking a repository and making a pull request by contributing to an open-source project, namely the GitHub repository with the source code for this tutorial. The GitHub repository can be found at https://github.com/thomas-rasmussen/git-tutorial.
Find a spelling or grammar error in the source code2, fix it, and make a pull request. Alternatively, if you are not familiar with websites built using Quarto, you can just make a random change.
Step 1 - Fork and clone the repository
Fork and clone the repository using either the web UI or the GitHub CLI.






TipHint





You can fork a repository using the gh repo fork command. See https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_fork for documentation on how to use the command.









NoteSolution





To fork and clone the repository at the same time using the GitHub CLI, use the following command:
# cd to an appropriate directory before forking and cloning the repository. Here we choose the home directory. 
$ cd
$ gh repo fork thomas-rasmussesn/git-tutorial  --clone




Step 2 - Implement change

title: 14  Rebasing
text:
14.1 Example
The commit history of a Git repository is not always pretty. If you commit often you might have a lot of small “WIP”, bug fix, typo, and refactor commits. Furthermore, if you use a branching workflow, as introduced in Chapter 5 (which you definitely should), you might also have a lot of merge commits which makes the commit history even more complicated. Ideally, we would like a simple linear commit history, where each commit is a meaningful change. It is impossible to get everything right in the first try, so what other tools does Git provide to help us with this? This is where rebasing comes into play. Rebasing allows you to rewrite the history of commits in a repository, by reapplying commits on top of another starting point, editing them while you do so. Rebasing has a reputation for being magical hocus pocus that beginners should stay away from, but it is an essential tool to manage a repository, especially when collaborating with others.
After rebasing we can now do a simple fast-forward merge to incorporate the changes from feature into main.
As noted above, it is important to stress that rebasing changes the commit history. In this example, C3 and C4 was originally applied onto C1, but after the rebase they are applied to C2, which at the very minimum will change the parent commit in the metadata of the commit object, and thus will result in new checksums.
Now that we have a basic understanding of what rebasing is, let’s see how to do it in practice. First, let’s set up a repository with a commit history akin to commit history in the illustration above:
As in the illustration in the start of the chapter, we want to rebase the commits on feature onto main. To do this we can use the git rebase command. Using the form git rebase <branch> Git will rebase the active branch (the branch HEAD is pointing to) onto <branch>:
In this simple example, Git will successfully rebase the commits on feature onto main without any additional input. Let’s look at the commit history after the rebase:
As expected we can see that the commit ID of the C3 and C4 commit has changed, while the commit ID of C1 and C2 has stayed the same.

title: 14  Rebasing

$ mkdir ~/rebase-example
$ cd ~/rebase-example
$ git init
$ touch file1.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"C1"
$ git switch -c feature
$ touch file3.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"C3"
$ touch file4.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"C4"
$ git switch main
$ touch file2.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"C2"
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
* 26806c3 (HEAD -> main) C2
| * 3aa6d72 (feature) C4
| * 1e8657b C3
|/
* 7639344 C1



$ git switch feature
$ git rebase main


git log --oneline --graph --all
* d5843e4 (HEAD -> feature) C4
* ffd1adb C3
* 26806c3 (main) C2
* 7639344 C1

title: 14  Rebasing
text:
14.2 Interactive rebasing
So far we have talked about (standard) Git rebasing. As you have seen, rebasing can be used to replay commits from one branch onto another branch. But rebasing is way more flexible than than just doing that. Using the -i flag, we can do interactive rebasing, which gives us more options. For example, we can split or combine commits while rebasing. Let see how this look like in practice. Imagine that we have implemented a feature in a series of commits in a feature branch that we want to merge into the main branch:
$ mkdir ~/rebase-squash
$ cd ~/rebase-squash
$ git init
$ echo "README" > README.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"Initial commit"
$ git switch -c add-new-feature
$ echo "Implementation of feature" > file.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"First draft of implementation"
$ echo "Fix a bug" >> file.txt
$ git commit -am"Fix bug"
$ echo "Refactor code" >> file.txt
$ git commit -am"Refactor to make more effecient"
$ git log --oneline
321b893 (HEAD -> add-new-feature) Refactor to make more efficient
83f522f Fix bug
86adade First draft of implementation
dc71be8 (main) Initial commit

We could simply do a fast-forward merge to integrate the changes from feature into main, but as is almost always the case, the individual commits on the feature branch are not that interesting in themselves, and are a product of trial and error while developing the feature. In a perfect world we would have been able to implement the entire feature in a single commit without having to fix any bugs or inefficient code. We can rewrite the history of the development of the feature by squashing the three commits on the feature branch into a single commit using interactive rebasing:
$ git rebase -i main

This command opens a file in your file editor that looks like this:

git-rebase-todo

pick 86adade # First draft of implementation
pick 83f522f # Fix bug
pick 321b893 # Refactor to make more efficient
# Rebase dc71be8..321b893 onto dc71be8 (3 commands)
#
# Commands:
# p, pick <commit> = use commit
# r, reword <commit> = use commit, but edit the commit message
# e, edit <commit> = use commit, but stop for amending
# s, squash <commit> = use commit, but meld into previous commit
# f, fixup [-C | -c] <commit> = like "squash" but keep only the previous
#                    commit's log message, unless -C is used, in which case
#                    keep only this commit's message; -c is same as -C but
#                    opens the editor
# x, exec <command> = run command (the rest of the line) using shell
# b, break = stop here (continue rebase later with 'git rebase --continue')
# d, drop <commit> = remove commit
# l, label <label> = label current HEAD with a name
# t, reset <label> = reset HEAD to a label
# m, merge [-C <commit> | -c <commit>] <label> [# <oneline>]
#         create a merge commit using the original merge commit's
#         message (or the oneline, if no original merge commit was
#         specified); use -c <commit> to reword the commit message
# u, update-ref <ref> = track a placeholder for the <ref> to be updated
#                       to this position in the new commits. The <ref> is
#                       updated at the end of the rebase
#
# These lines can be re-ordered; they are executed from top to bottom.
#
# If you remove a line here THAT COMMIT WILL BE LOST.
#
# However, if you remove everything, the rebase will be aborted.
#



The file starts by listing the commits that are to be rebased and in what order they will be applied to the main branch. As stated near the bottom of the file, we can actually reorder the commits to replay them in a different order. Furthermore, we are informed of different actions we can do while applying each commit. By default, the “pick” option is chosen, which will simply apply the patch of changes in the commit. The option we are looking for here is the “squash” option, which will meld a commit into the previous commit. So to combine the three commits into a single commit we can edit the file to look like this:

git-rebase-todo

pick 86adade # First draft of implementation
squash 83f522f # Fix bug
squash 321b893 # Refactor to make more efficient



We have removed the comments here to reduce the size of the output, but you don’t have to do that. We save and close the file, and another file will open, giving us a chance we alter the commit message:

COMMIT_EDITMSG

# This is a combination of 3 commits.
# This is the 1st commit message:

First draft of implementation

# This is the commit message #2:

Fix bug

# This is the commit message #3:

Refactor to make more efficient

# Please enter the commit message for your changes. Lines starting
# with '#' will be ignored, and an empty message aborts the commit.
#
# Date:      Thu Aug 13 14:38:20 2026 +0200
#
# interactive rebase in progress; onto dc71be8
# Last commands done (3 commands done):
#    squash 83f522f # Fix bug
#    squash 321b893 # Refactor to make more efficient
# No commands remaining.
# You are currently rebasing branch 'add-new-feature' on 'dc71be8'.
#
# Changes to be committed:
#       new file:   file.txt
#



By default the commit message is a concatenation of the individual commit messages, and we can use that as a starting point to draft a more appropriate commit message:

COMMIT_EDITMSG

Implement feature



Again, we save and close the file. Git now does the rebasing, and we are done. Let’s look at the commit history again:
$ git log --oneline
3df4aa8 (HEAD -> add-new-feature) Implement feature
dc71be8 (main) Initial commit

We have now rewritten the history of commits, so that it looks like we implemented the feature perfectly in a single commit, and we can do a simple fast-forward merge to integrate the changes into the main branch.
As you might be able to grasp at this point, you can rewrite your commit history entirely as you see fit. Replaying commits from one branch to another, and squashing commits are some of the most common uses of rebasing, but this is, as always, only scraping the surface of what you can do with rebasing.

title: 14  Rebasing
text:
14.3 Handling merge conflicts while rebasing
So far we have only considered trivial examples where we have no merge conflicts. If there is a merge conflict during rebasing, git rebase will stop at the time of the first conflict, add conflict markers to the files with conflicting changes, and give control back to the user to resolve the conflict, before moving forward with the rebase. During this process, Git will provide details on what to do and how, but generally speaking you resolve the conflict by editing files, use git add to mark the conflicts as resolved, and then use git rebase --continue to continue the rebasing process. During a rebase it is also possible to abort the process and return to the state of the repository before starting the rebase using git rebase --abort. Let’s illustrate a merge conflict during a rebase with an example. Consider the following repository:




Repository before rebasing



Which can be created with the following commmands:
$ mkdir ~/rebase-merge-conflict
$ cd rebase-merge-conflict
$ git init
$ echo "First commit on main branch" > file.txt
$ git add .
$ git commit -m"First commit on main branch"
$ git switch -c feature
$ echo "Commit on feature branch" >> file.txt
$ git commit -am"Commit on feature branch"
$ git switch main
$ echo "Second commit on main branch" >> file.txt
$ git commit -am"Second commit on main branch"
$ git log --oneline --all --graph
* b744d7b (HEAD -> main) Second commit on main branch
| * 6f7e6de (feature) Commit on feature branch
|/
* 87d57f0 First commit on main branch

We want to rebase the feature branch onto the main branch, but when we try to do this we get the following feedback from Git:
$ git switch feature
$ git rebase main
Auto-merging file.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in file.txt
error: could not apply 6f7e6de... Commit on feature branch
hint: Resolve all conflicts manually, mark them as resolved with
hint: "git add/rm ", then run "git rebase --continue".
hint: You can instead skip this commit: run "git rebase --skip".
hint: To abort and get back to the state before "git rebase", run "git rebase --abort".
hint: Disable this message with "git config set advice.mergeConflict false"
Could not apply 6f7e6de... # Commit on feature branch


Git helpfully informs us that we have a merge conflict in file.txt. Normally, you would open file.txt in a text editor and resolve the conflict, but here we will just remake the file in the terminal, including the changes from both branches:
$ cat file.txt
First commit on main branch
<<<<<<< HEAD
Second commit on main branch
=======
Commit on feature branch
>>>>>>> 6f7e6de (Commit on feature branch)
$ echo "First commit on main branch" > file.txt
$ echo "Second commit on main branch" >> file.txt
$ echo "Commit on feature branch" >> file.txt
$ cat file.txt
First commit on main branch
Second commit on main branch
Commit on feature branch

We can now use git add and continue the rebase with git rebase --continue as instructed:
$ git add .
$ git rebase --continue

This will finalize the rebase, and Git opens a file for us to edit the commit message for the rebased commit, which we simply keep as “Commit on feature branch”. The commit history now looks as following:
git log --oneline --graph --oneline
* a0daf9d (HEAD -> feature) Commit on feature branch
* b744d7b (main) Second commit on main branch
* 87d57f0 First commit on main branch

Which is also illustrated in the diagram below:




Repository after rebasing



We end this example with cleaning up:
$ cd
$ rm rebase-merge-conflict -rf
